title: What is the Circuit Breaker pattern, how does Resilience4j implement it, how does it differ from Retry, and what is the default aspect-order gotcha (Retry wrapping CircuitBreaker, `CallNotPermittedException`)?
shortTitle: What is the Circuit Breaker pattern, how does Resilience4j implement it, how does it differ from Retry, and what is the default aspect-order gotcha
keyPoints: A circuit breaker stops a service from repeatedly calling a failing dependency by failing fast after a threshold.
Resilience4j models it as CLOSED (calls pass) -> OPEN (calls fail fast) -> HALF_OPEN (trial calls test recovery).
The sliding window can be count-based (last 100 calls) or time-based (last 10 seconds).
Retry just re-attempts a failed call; it is for transient glitches, not sustained failures.
The default aspect order makes Retry outermost wrapping CircuitBreaker, so Retry retries the open circuit's CallNotPermittedException.
Fix: reorder so CircuitBreaker wraps Retry, or tell Retry to ignore CallNotPermittedException.
Always pair a circuit breaker with a timeout, because a breaker cannot trip on calls that never return.

s1_definition.oneliner: A circuit breaker trips open after too many failures so calls fail fast, Resilience4j runs it as a CLOSED-OPEN-HALF_OPEN state machine, Retry just re-attempts, and by default Retry wraps CircuitBreaker so it wastefully retries the open circuit's CallNotPermittedException.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Circuit breaker** – A stability mechanism that tracks recent failure rate and, once it crosses a threshold, opens to reject calls instantly instead of hanging.
- **Three states** – CLOSED (calls pass, outcomes recorded), OPEN (calls rejected with CallNotPermittedException), HALF_OPEN (trial calls test recovery).
- **Sliding window** – Count-based (last N calls) or time-based (last N seconds) for computing the failure rate.
- **Retry** – A separate pattern that re-attempts a failed call a bounded number of times with backoff; for transient glitches.
- **Aspect-order gotcha** – By default Retry wraps CircuitBreaker, so Retry sees the open circuit's exception as another failure and retries pointlessly.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's app calls an external credit-score service. If that service is down, calling it again and again wastes time and ties up threads. A circuit breaker is like a smart fuse: after too many failures it trips and immediately says "do not even try right now", so customers get a fast fallback. After a cooling-off period it cautiously lets one call through to test recovery. The gotcha is that if the retry logic is outside the fuse, it keeps flipping the fuse switch even after it has tripped.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Circuit Breaker State Machine:

         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │              CLOSED                     │
         │  Calls pass through normally            │
         │  Outcomes recorded in sliding window    │
         │  Failure rate: 30%                      │
         └──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                        │ failure rate > 50%
                        ▼
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │              OPEN                       │
         │  All calls REJECTED immediately         │
         │  CallNotPermittedException thrown        │
         │  Wait duration: 30 seconds              │
         └──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                        │ wait duration expires
                        ▼
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │           HALF_OPEN                     │
         │  3 trial calls permitted                │
         │  If succeed -> back to CLOSED           │
         │  If fail -> back to OPEN                │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Aspect Order:
  WRONG:   Retry ──▶ CircuitBreaker ──▶ Call
           (retries open circuit's exception)

  CORRECT: CircuitBreaker ──▶ Retry ──▶ Call
           (open circuit fails fast, retry only inside closed)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Circuit Breaker pattern stops a service from repeatedly calling a dependency that is failing. When a downstream is slow or down, naive callers keep sending requests that each wait for a timeout, consuming threads until the caller itself fails. The breaker watches outcomes and, once failures are frequent enough, opens so calls fail fast with a fallback, giving the dependency room to recover.

Resilience4j implements this as a three-state machine. CLOSED: calls pass through, outcomes recorded in a sliding window. When the failure rate crosses the threshold, it transitions to OPEN, where every call is rejected with CallNotPermittedException. After a wait duration, it moves to HALF_OPEN to test recovery. Retry is a complementary pattern for transient glitches, not sustained failure. The two combine: Retry absorbs brief blips, the breaker protects against prolonged outages.

The gotcha Pankaj learned at National Bank of India is the default aspect order: Retry wraps CircuitBreaker, so when the circuit is open, Retry sees the CallNotPermittedException and wastefully retries against an open circuit. The fix is to reorder so CircuitBreaker wraps Retry, which means once the circuit opens, the whole call fails fast with zero wasted retries. Also always pair the breaker with a timeout, because a breaker cannot trip on calls that never return.

Remember one sentence: a circuit breaker trips open after too many failures so calls fail fast, Retry merely re-attempts transient failures, and you must reorder their aspects so the breaker is outermost or the retry wastes time against an open circuit.
